It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses those two `max()` paddings, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's inset to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too); a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. So that nothing scrolls into view above it, under the host's controls, paint that band with `body::before { content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10; background: ... }`, in the header's own background where the header opens the page and in the page's where the sticky bar starts lower. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside the `:root` padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets the `:root` padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

Here's how a two-die button press works, based on the search results.

**Setup:** The machine has a pickup die and a crimp die, mounted on a rotating table. The button maker has three main sections: the Pick-up Die (Stage 1), the Magnet & Upper Die, and the Crimp Die (Stage 2). The pin back goes in the crimp die, and the metal shell goes in the pickup die.

**Steps:**
- **Load the shell:** The shell goes into the pickup die with its sharp edge pointing down, and the design goes on top, followed by a clear mylar film. Insert a shell into the pickup die with the sharp edge facing downward. Place the graphic on the shell. Place the mylar on top of the graphic.
- **Load the backing:** Place a pinned back into the crimp die with the sharp edge facing up.
- **First press (pickup):** The pickup die is rotated under the upper die. Pull the handle down, crimping the shell, graphic and mylar into the upper die. Raising the handle then lifts the assembled layers up into the upper die.
- **Second press (crimp):** Raise the handle and rotate the crimp die counter-clockwise. With the pin back still in the crimp die, pull the handle a second time. This joins the front and back, and the finished button is removed by rotating the table again.

**Mechanism:** Sources describe the press as a die system that applies even pressure to form a round badge. One patent describes the punch and die arrangement in more detail. The shell and artwork are partially pushed out of the punch and into the second die. Continued downward punch motion overcomes the crimp ring springs, pushing the shell and artwork over the badge back. The spring-loaded crimp ring is what lets the edges of the shell fold over the backing.

**Tips from the guides:** Make sure only one shell is loaded, since shells can stick together. Discard dented shells, because they won't crimp fully. Also, make sure all parts of the image you want to be visible are contained within the button face line, and the remaining image edge folds around the back.

## Patent Details
- **Title:** Die set apparatus for badges
- **Patent:** US 4,696,086 A
- **Inventor:** John W. Dickerson
- **Assignee:** Listed as "Individual" (no corporate assignee)
- **Filed:** January 22, 1986
- **Granted/published:** September 29, 1987
- **Status:** Expired, due to nonpayment of maintenance fees (effective 1991)

## Components
Your terms map to the patent as follows:
- **Upper punch:** A punch block attached to the ram, with a spring-loaded punch ring that slides on the block hub. The punch ring hub extends past the block face to form a recess.
- **Lower pickup die (first die):** An anvil with a flat support surface, surrounded by an annular groove and a retainer ring that centers the artwork.
- **Crimp die (second die):** A base with a hub and a recess for the badge pin, plus a spring-loaded crimp ring with a counterbore and tapered surface.

## Springs and Dimensions
- **Punch springs:** Preloaded to about 100 lb at a 0.50 in minimum gap between the block flange and punch ring disk.
- **Crimp springs:** About 350 lb at a 0.13 in clearance between the base flange and crimp ring. The patent states the crimp springs are always stiffer than the punch springs.

The results give three different formulas, and they disagree because each source measures the toggle angle from a different reference line. All of them come from FIRGELLI's engineering blog, a vendor of linear actuators, so none is an independent textbook derivation.

- **Angle measured from horizontal:** The calculator page gives Fout = Fin / tan(θ), so MA = Fout / Fin = 1 / tan(θ).
- **Angle measured from the dead-centre line:** The toggle mechanism article uses F_out = F_in / (2 * tan(theta)); MA = 1 / (2 * tan(theta)), with the assumptions that the input acts perpendicular to the link line and that ideal frictionless pins are assumed. The factor of 2 reflects the symmetric two-link geometry.
- **Double-toggle screw press:** The press page models the toggle multiplier as M_toggle = 1 / sin(theta), with θ measured from the straight dead-centre position. The double-toggle article gives the same MA = 1 / sin(theta) and states that at roughly 5° from straight, force at the ram is about 5× the screw thrust.

For a hand-lever toggle press, the 1/sin form with θ measured from dead centre is the most relevant. Check the convention before using any formula, and verify the result with a free-body diagram that accounts for friction and pin losses, since these sources ignore them. The sources also note that most designs stick to about 10–30°, which keeps the mechanical advantage useful without making the press too sensitive to small angle errors.

**Patent:** US 6,038,944 A, "Apparatus for manufacturing buttons"
**Assignee:** Tecre Co., Inc. (original assignee; inventor Benjamin A. Braunberger)
**Dates:** Filed July 24, 1997; published March 21, 2000. Status: expired.

**Press frame types**
- *Prior art:* The Parisian Novelty machine and the Technical Products machines use C-shaped frames. The Parisian frame needs "a heavy and complicated cast metal structure." The Instant Buttons machine uses an H-shaped frame.
- *Invention:* A "sturdy but simple and inexpensive box frame" with a base, a hollow center column, an end column, and a crown.

**Die mounting**
- *Prior art:* Parisian uses a turntable indexable about 90 degrees. Technical Products uses a reciprocating slide, or a stacked, invertible die arrangement. Instant Buttons uses a reciprocating slide.
- *Invention:* A die table that rotates about the center column through 180 degrees. Cutouts at its ends contact the end column to locate it at both positions. A pickup die sits on one end and a crimp die on the other.

**Handle and linkage**
- A handle is pivotally connected to the crown. Its two plates straddle the crown and end in a hand grip, with cam surfaces that press down on the ram plate.
- A spring biases the ram plate upward against the crown.
- The ram outer ring carries two pins and two fingers about 30 degrees apart. A shifter post on the die table rotates the outer ring between pickup and crimp modes.
- A clearance between the pins and the ram plate must be taken up before the outer ring advances during a pickup stroke.

**Tipping problem and solution**
- *Problem:* In the Instant Buttons design, the ram handle falls outside the machine base, so "the entire machine tends to tip over with every handle stroke."
- *Solution:* At the end of the crimp stroke the grip sits over the base. As the patent puts it, "Having the handle grip over the machine base prevents the machine from tipping over."

**Forces**
- No numeric force values are given. The patent says only that the final crimp requires "a moderate force" on the handle grip.

**Dimensions**
- Trophy recess seats are 1 inch or 2 inches in diameter (25 mm or 50 mm in European trophies).
- The die table indexes 180 degrees in the preferred embodiment.
- The flat back is about 0.04 inches thick (hard plastic is preferred; metal is also possible).

**Materials**
- Formed backs are usually steel.
- Flat backs may be metal or hard plastic.
- The patent does not specify the frame material.

# Two-Stroke Machine for Making Buttons Having Coplanar Shell Flanges

**Title:** Two-stroke machine for making buttons having coplanar shell flanges
**Patent:** US 6,938,518 B1
**Assignee:** Tecre Co Inc (later listed as Tecre Company Inc.)
**Inventor:** Benjamin A. Braunberger
**Application:** No. 10/342,064, filed January 14, 2003
**Published/granted:** September 6, 2005
**Listed status:** Expired, lifetime (adjusted expiration July 23, 2023, per the page's legal-status note, which is not a legal conclusion)

## Rectangular Button Construction

- **Shell:** Sheet metal about 0.008 to 0.009 inches thick, with four free edges and clipped corners. Each edge has a metal margin that is bent into a flange.
- **Flat back:** Rectangular, made of metal or plastic, and flat over its whole area.
- **Laminate:** A printed graphic covered by a transparent protective film such as polyester.
- **Assembly:** The laminate's skirt overhangs the shell edges, is tucked between the shell margins and the back's periphery, and the margins are bent into flanges lying in one plane parallel to the back. The patent says this gives a more secure, finished result than the older angled margins.

The page gives little detail on corners beyond the clipped shell corners.

## Die and Ram Design

**Pickup die:**
- A pedestal fastened to the die table, with a flat top, four external shoulders, and four slightly drafted side surfaces.
- An outer frame that slides over the pedestal, biased away from the die table by several pickup springs. Its top has a recess for the laminate and internal surfaces that center the shell.

**Crimp die:**
- A pedestal with a top surface, an external shoulder, and a relief surface parallel to and spaced from the top.
- An outer frame biased by crimp die springs, with a top recess and a bevel between the recess and the inner surface. The bevel is preferably concave and scalloped.
- Spring cells in bores in the outer frame's underside. Each has a very stiff spring and a plunger that rests on the die table when the frame bottoms out. These cells are the key change that allows two strokes instead of three.

**Ram die:**
- A rectangular plug with a concave-lipped working face, fixed to the carrier's guide bar.
- A four-sided ram frame that slides on the plug over a distance D. Downward travel is limited by support-block overhangs.
- Inner surfaces with shallow scalloped grooves, which hold the bent shell margins during transfer.
- Pins pressed into the frame's top surface, parallel to the ram axis, protruding slightly less than D.

**Carrier:** A guide bar plus a shifter cage that rotates on the bar. The cage has holes at the same radius as the frame pins.

## Operating Strokes

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-0/bundled-skills/2.1.310/ecaec9d4ea0696cddd3055ab75f24bf7/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

content.content:
# Marks & anatomy

The quiet, considered look is a few fixed specs plus two pieces of negative space.
The data is the only thing allowed to be loud.

## Mark specs (fixed across every chart)

| Mark | Spec |
|---|---|
| Bar / column | **<= 24px thick** (cap it - never fill the slot; let the band's leftover be air); **4px rounded data-end, square at the baseline**; grows from a single baseline |
| Line | **2px**, round join/cap |
| Marker / end-dot | **>= 8px** (r >= 4), filled with the series color |
| Area fill | the series hue at **~10% opacity** (a wash, never a saturated block) |
| Gridlines / axes | one-step-off-surface gray, **hairline (1px), solid** (never dashed), recessive |

## The two spacers (white doing the separating)

- **Surface gap.** A **2px gap** in the surface color separates touching marks - every
  segment of a stacked bar, and every adjacent (touching) bar, the same width. Keep it
  one consistent width across a stack; neighbors one step apart read distinct because of
  the gap, not a stroke drawn around them.
- **Surface ring.** Dots and end-markers carry a **2px ring in the surface color**,
  so they stay legible where they cross a line or overlap each other. The ring is part
  of the mark's hover/hit target, not just spacing - see `interaction.md` (small dots
  are easy to under-size for hover).

Never draw a border around a mark to separate it. The gap and the ring are the
mechanism; a stroke adds data-weight ink that isn't data.

## Labels & legend

A **legend is always present for two or more series** - the dependable identity
channel; never make the reader rely on color-matching alone. Direct labels then ride
the marks to *supplement* it. **A single series needs no legend box**: there is only
one color, so the chart's title or subtitle already says what is plotted. A box with
one swatch restates the title and costs space.

- **Label selectively - never a number on every point.** A value beside every dot or
  segment is chaos and goes unread. Label the endpoint, the extreme, or the one series
  the story is about; let the axis, the legend, and the tooltip/table carry the rest.
  Direct labels work *because* they are sparing - flood the chart and they stop working.
- **Direct labels before gridlines; gridlines before a second axis.**
- **A label that won't fit doesn't get clipped - measure first.** Only place a label
  *inside* a bar or stacked segment when the rendered text fits with comfortable
  padding on both sides. If it doesn't fit: for a whole bar/column, move the label
  outside the bar end (or to the tooltip if there's no room outside either); for an
  *interior* stacked segment (which has no free end),
  skip the inline label and let the legend + tooltip carry it. Either way the value
  stays in the table view, so nothing is gated. Never use `overflow: hidden` on the
  segment to "solve" it - that crops the first/last characters and is worse than no
  label. Text never overflows or is clipped by its own mark.
- Bars -> value at the tip. Columns -> value on the cap. Lines -> value at the end.
- Y-axis ticks: round to clean numbers, compact from 1,000 up (0 / 1K / 2K); they
  carry the values you didn't directly label, so keep them unless every value is labeled.
- **Text never wears the data color.** Marks - bars, lines, dots, area fills - carry
  the series color; labels, values, legends, and axis text use **text tokens**
  (primary / secondary / muted). A light categorical hue (yellow, aqua) is illegible
  as text on the surface. Identity comes from the colored mark *beside* the text - a
  dot, a short line-key, a swatch - never from coloring the text itself. A label set
  *inside* a colored fill (a stacked segment, a map tile) is the one exception: white or
  near-black, the same two in both modes, by the fill's luminance. `palette.md` says which its
  categorical and status colors take.
- **When end-labels collide, don't stack them.** Direct end-labels work when series

# Marks & anatomy

The quiet, considered look is a few fixed specs plus two pieces of negative space.
The data is the only thing allowed to be loud.

## Mark specs (fixed across every chart)

| Mark | Spec |
|---|---|
| Bar / column | **<= 24px thick** (cap it - never fill the slot; let the band's leftover be air); **4px rounded data-end, square at the baseline**; grows from a single baseline |
| Line | **2px**, round join/cap |
| Marker / end-dot | **>= 8px** (r >= 4), filled with the series color |
| Area fill | the series hue at **~10% opacity** (a wash, never a saturated block) |
| Gridlines / axes | one-step-off-surface gray, **hairline (1px), solid** (never dashed), recessive |

## The two spacers (white doing the separating)

- **Surface gap.** A **2px gap** in the surface color separates touching marks - every
  segment of a stacked bar, and every adjacent (touching) bar, the same width. Keep it
  one consistent width across a stack; neighbors one step apart read distinct because of
  the gap, not a stroke drawn around them.
- **Surface ring.** Dots and end-markers carry a **2px ring in the surface color**,
  so they stay legible where they cross a line or overlap each other. The ring is part
  of the mark's hover/hit target, not just spacing - see `interaction.md` (small dots
  are easy to under-size for hover).

Never draw a border around a mark to separate it. The gap and the ring are the
mechanism; a stroke adds data-weight ink that isn't data.

## Labels & legend

A **legend is always present for two or more series** - the dependable identity

one swatch restates the title and costs space.

  segment is chaos and goes unread. Label the endpoint, the extreme, or the one series
  the story is about; let the axis, the legend, and the tooltip/table carry the rest.

- **A label that won't fit doesn't get clipped - measure first.** Only place a label

Design pack · manual photo-magnet press

MagPress M4

A hand-lever toggle press with a sliding two-station die table. It makes square and rectangular photo fridge magnets in two strokes, and its four die sets swap without tools. This page has the 3D model, the force analysis, die and frame dimensions, a parts list, the manufacturing route, assembly steps and test plan.

Sizes50×50 · 63.5×63.5
53×80 · 65×90
Unitsmm, N, kN
DriveToggle, MA 6 → 31
Die force5.6 kN @ 200 N hand
RevisionA · 2026-10-26
StatusFor prototype
01

3D model

Drag to orbit · scroll or pinch to zoom · click a part to inspect it
Loading the 3D model…
Die set (magnet size, mm)
Press cycle
65°
Die table
View
Step 1 / 9

0%

Take the model further

The OpenSCAD copy is the full assembly with the selected die set, built from simple solids at true size. Use it as a starting layout in OpenSCAD, then import it into FreeCAD or Fusion to detail it.

02

How it makes a magnet

Each magnet takes two strokes of the handle. The die table slides between two stations. Each lower die is loaded while it is outside the press, so your fingers are never under the ram. The upper die stays on the ram and does both jobs. This is the slide-type layout from the photo you sent. The two-stroke die action follows the badge-press patents listed in section 12, all expired.

    Layer stack, front to back

    Mylar film (0.075 mm PET) → printed photo (120–150 g/m² matte paper) → tinplate shell (0.20–0.23 mm, drawn tray with clipped corners) → back plate (1.0–1.5 mm ABS/acrylic, or cardboard) → adhesive magnet sheet, applied after pressing.

    Sellers ship slightly different stacks (cardboard backs, acrylic backs, tin backs). The die set and the consumables must match, so buy consumables to this pack's sizes or adjust the die values in section 05.

    Why these choices
    • Toggle, not cam: force rises as the stroke closes, which is where crimping needs it. The stroke ends 8° before dead centre, so it can't lock over.
    • H-frame with two columns: it is symmetric, so the ram can't tilt under load the way a C-frame does.
    • Slide, not turntable: it is simpler to make. Stop blocks give repeatable positions, and the table can't drift while you press.
    • Grip lands over the base tongue: the press can't tip toward you at the end of the stroke.
    • Keyed die shoes: the A and B shoes have different dowel patterns, so they can't go on the wrong station.
    03

    Specification

    ItemValueBasis
    Magnet sizes50×50, 63.5×63.5, 53×80, 65×90One swappable die set per size: an upper die and lower dies A and B
    Strokes per magnet2Pickup, then crimp
    Ram stroke38.9 mmToggle crank 40, link 60, handle 65° → 3°
    Open gap above lower die26 mmClearance for the table to slide with parts loaded
    Die working zonelast 12.9 mmFrom die contact to the end of the stroke
    Force at die, end of stroke5.6 kN200 N on the grip, 90% pin efficiency (section 04)
    Frame design load8 kNCovers a 280 N push. Crown stress ≈ 90 MPa, deflection ≈ 0.12 mm
    Footprint (W × D)460 × 470 mmBase 460 × 260 plus front tongue 210. The table overhangs 20 mm at each end stop
    Height≈ 260 closed, ≈ 550 handle upHandle 350 mm from the pivot
    Mass (estimate)≈ 28 kgSteel base, crown and ram. About 20 kg if the base is cut from 10 mm plate and the ram from 7075
    Die change≈ 2–3 min, no tools1 lock screw on the upper die, 2 thumb screws per lower die
    Output (estimate)2–4 magnets/minPractised operator. Measure on the prototype
    04

    Force through the stroke

    The handle drives a toggle. The crank (O→A, 40 mm) and the link (A→B, 60 mm) straighten as the handle comes down. Ram movement per degree of handle travel shrinks toward the bottom, so the force multiplies, reaching about ×31 at the end. Mechanical advantage is MA = L / (dy/dφ) with dy/dφ = a·sinφ + a²·sinφ·cosφ / √(b² − a²sin²φ), where L = 290 mm (pivot to grip centre), a = 40, b = 60, and φ is the crank angle from straight down. The chart assumes 200 N on the grip and 90% efficiency through the three pins.

    The required force for each die set is an estimate: about 7 N per mm of magnet edge for the crimp spring preload, scaled from the round-badge spring figures in US 4,696,086, then × 2.2 for the final crimp. Measure it on the prototype with a load cell (section 10). Stroke 1 needs much less force and stops at about 35.5 mm, when the plug meets the shell.

    05

    Swappable die sets

    Common interface, same on all four sets
    • Upper die: Ø16 g6 shank with a flat, fitted into the Ø16 H7 die holder and locked by one M6 side screw. A Ø4 pin in a slot fixes the rotation, which matters for rectangles. A ground shim pack on each upper die sets its depth once, so swapping needs no adjustment.
    • Lower dies: each sits on a 130 × 140 × 10 shoe with two Ø8 dowels and two M6 thumb screws. Shoe A has its dowels on the X axis; shoe B has them on the Z axis.
    • Marking: shoe A has a green band and is laser-marked "A · PICKUP". Shoe B has a red band and "B · CRIMP". Each part carries the size code, for example M4-6390.
    Materials
    • Production: 1.2379 / Cr12MoV (D2 type), vacuum hardened and tempered to 58–60 HRC. Wire-EDM the profiles after hardening, grind the faces, and polish the forming edges to Ra 0.2–0.4 µm. Optional TiN or hard-chrome coat.
    • Prototype: 7075-T6 aluminium, CNC machined and hard anodised. This is the cheapest way to prove the fits. Expect faster wear on the forming edges.
    • Shoes: 6061-T6 or C45. Springs: ISO 10243 die springs, colour-coded green (light) for A, blue (medium) for the upper frame, red or yellow (strong) for B.

    Fits are starting values. Upper frame opening = shell + 0.35 mm, so it grips the wrapped shell by friction. Plug = shell + 0.30 mm, sliding in the frame. Crimp frame opening = shell + 0.45 mm. Lap the upper frame opening on the first prototype until a wrapped shell lifts out of die A reliably and pushes out cleanly over die B.

    Consumables per die set

    06

    Frame and drive parts

    One frame serves all four die sets. Base, crown and ram carry the column holes at 210.00 mm pitch. Machine all three with the same program and datum scheme, or line-bore them together, so the ram slides freely once the column nuts are torqued.

    07

    Bill of materials

    Budget guide (rough, 2026)
    • Frame and drive parts, one prototype from a local CNC shop: about $600–1,200.
    • Bought parts (bushings, springs, pins, fasteners, grip, feet): about $80–150.
    • Die set in 7075 aluminium: about $120–300 each. In hardened Cr12MoV: about $250–600 each.
    • Batch pricing (10+) and shops in India or China usually cost much less. Get three quotes from this drawing pack.
    Make or buy

    Make the frame, drive and dies; they are simple prismatic parts that any 3-axis CNC shop and wire-EDM shop can handle. Buy everything that is a catalogue item: bushings, die springs, pins, fasteners, ball plungers, thumb screws, grip and feet. Buy consumables (shells, film, backs, magnet sheet) from a magnet-supplies vendor in the four sizes.

    08

    Manufacturing route

    Part familyRouteCritical checks
    Base plateLaser or plasma cut 12 mm S235 → stress-relieve if it warps → CNC face the station area → bore columns → drill and tap → powder coat with masksFlatness 0.05 under the die table; column holes Ø25 H7 at 210.00 ±0.01
    Crown, ram, cheeks, clevisSaw C45 bar → CNC mill and bore (same datum and program as the base) → deburr → black oxideColumn and bushing holes square to the faces within 0.02/100
    ColumnsTurn GCr15 → induction harden 58–62 HRC → centreless grind Ø25 h6 → hard chrome 10 µm → thread endsStraight within 0.02 over length; Ra ≤ 0.4
    Toggle parts (hub, links)Wire EDM or CNC from C45 plate → ream Ø12 H7 → black oxideCentre distances 40.00 and 60.00 ±0.02; links matched as a pair
    PinsBuy as hardened dowel stock Ø12 g6, or turn GCr15 → harden → grind → retaining-ring groovesPin to bore clearance 0.01–0.03
    Die table, shoesCNC 6061-T6 → ream dowel holes → Helicoils → hard anodise (table gold)Table flat 0.03; dowel holes true position 0.02
    Dies, productionSaw Cr12MoV → CNC rough with 0.3 mm left → vacuum harden 1020–1040 °C, gas quench, temper twice → 58–60 HRC → wire EDM the profiles (plug, frame openings, pedestals) → surface grind → polish forming edges and bevel → optional TiNProfile ±0.01; plug-to-frame sliding fit 0.02–0.03 per side; forming edges Ra 0.2–0.4
    Dies, prototypeCNC 7075-T6 to size → hard anodise 25–50 µm (machine allowance for the coating) → polish edgesSame fits as production, measured after anodise
    MarkingLaser-mark size code, die letter and shim value on every die part. Paint the A and B bands on the shoesReadable after cleaning
    09

    Assembly

    Each step has a "Show in 3D" button that opens the build view at that step

      Swapping a die set

      1. Rest the handle fully up on its stop and slide the table so both stations are clear.
      2. Upper die: support it with one hand, loosen the M6 side screw on the die holder, and pull the die straight down. Push in the new die with the flat facing the screw and the pin in its slot, then tighten.
      3. Lower dies: loosen the two thumb screws on each shoe and lift the shoe off its dowels. Fit the new A shoe (green) on the left station and the new B shoe (red) on the right. The dowels prevent mix-ups.
      4. Make one slow dry stroke on each station with no parts. The upper frame's lead-in should enter both lower frames without touching.
      5. Make two test magnets and check the corners and the crimp before running a batch.
      10

      Setup, calibration and tests

      TestHowPass
      Station alignmentPut a Ø16 centring pin with a point in the die holder. Adjust each stop screw until the point lands on the station's centre mark. Lock the nuts.±0.05 mm at both stations
      Stroke and handle stopMeasure ram travel with calipers from handle-up to handle-down.38.9 ±0.3 mm; handle stops 3° above horizontal
      Depth (per die set)Fit the shims so the crimp finishes with the handle about 5–10° above horizontal. Record the shim value on the upper die.Full crimp with a firm push; no hard knock at the bottom
      ForcePut a load cell (10 kN button cell) on station B with a dummy block. Push the grip with a hanging scale at 200 N.≥ 5 kN; compare with section 04
      Magnet qualityMake 20 of each size.No white paper at the edges, no torn film, no corner wrinkles, flange flat and closed all round, back doesn't move under a firm thumb twist
      Drop and pullDrop five magnets from 1 m onto a hard floor; pull each back by hand.No separation (set your own stricter spec for sale)
      EnduranceRun 1,000 strokes, half on each station, then repeat the alignment and quality checks.No change in alignment, no galling on the columns
      Safety. The pinch points are between the upper and lower dies, and between the table and the stop blocks. Load parts only at the outer stations. Return springs hold the handle up when released. Wear cut-resistant gloves when handling loose tinplate shells. The press weighs about 28 kg, so use two people to lift it.
      11

content.text:
I've built the design pack for the press in your photo: a hand-lever photo-magnet press with all 4 sizes as swappable die sets.

**Open it here:** https://claude.ai/artifact/C4NaemzVJD5yDM3Ks2FCBi
The link is private for now. If you want to share it, use the page's Share menu.

The earlier printer idea never produced any files, so there was nothing to delete. Main stays blank, and the pack lives only at that link.

**What's in the pack**
- **3D model:** you can rotate it, drag the handle, slide the die table, and play the full cycle: load, stroke 1 (pickup), slide, stroke 2 (crimp), finished magnet. There is also an exploded view, a cut-away, and a 9-step build mode. Click any part to see its material, size and notes.
- **Die sets:** a table of every die dimension for all 4 sizes, a labelled cross-section of the dies, and the consumables per size (shell, photo cut size, film, back, magnet sheet).
- **Force chart:** at 200 N on the grip the press gives about 5.6 kN at the die. That covers the estimated need of 3.0–4.7 kN, depending on size.
- **Frame and drive parts:** materials and tolerances, a parts list (you can copy it as CSV), and a rough budget.
- **Build and test plan:** the machining route, assembly steps with checks, how to swap a die set, and a test plan.
- **OpenSCAD export:** a "Copy OpenSCAD" button gives you the whole assembly as a starting CAD model.

**Main design choices**
- **Two-column frame:** a sturdy frame with a toggle lever drive.
- **Sliding die table:** you load each die outside the press, so your hands are never under the ram.
- **Tool-free die swap:** the upper die is held by one screw, each lower die by two thumb screws, and dies A and B can't be fitted the wrong way round.
- **Anti-tip base:** the base has a front extension under the handle, so the press can't tip toward you.

**What still needs proving on a real prototype**
- **Force and spring numbers:** these are estimates scaled from expired badge-press patents. Measure them with a load cell, as the test plan describes.
- **Die fits:** these are starting values. Expect to hand-fit the upper die on the first prototype.
- **Consumables:** they must match the dies. Sellers' part stacks differ, so buy to the sizes in the pack.

**Research:** I found no open-source CAD for this kind of press. The design draws on three expired patents (Dickerson 1987, Tecre 2000 and 2005), published button-press guides, and seller listings for the 4 sizes. All sources are linked on the page. Before selling, have a patent agent check for current patents in your market.

**Checks:** I rendered the page in a test browser, ran the full press cycle, switched sizes, and checked it fits phone width with no errors. After that I brightened the metal and widened the default camera view, and I haven't looked at those two changes rendered.

Next I can produce proper 2D part drawings for a machine shop, or a STEP CAD model.

"""MagPress M4 part drawings. Coordinates: x right, y up, z toward the operator (front).
Plan views: u = x, w = -z (front at the bottom of the view) unless stated."""
import math
from draft import *

SIZES = [('5050', 50.0, 50.0), ('6363', 63.5, 63.5), ('5380', 80.0, 53.0), ('6590', 90.0, 65.0)]   # code, X (along table), Z
SIZE_LABEL = {'5050': '50 × 50', '6363': '63.5 × 63.5', '5380': '53 × 80', '6590': '65 × 90'}
SHOWN = ('6590', 90.0, 65.0)
GEN = ['General tolerances ISO 2768-mK; fits per ISO 286; threads ISO metric 6H/6g.',
       'Break all sharp edges 0.3 × 45° unless stated. Remove all burrs.']

SHEETS = []
DXFS = {}


def new(no, title, **kw):
    sh = Sheet(no, title, **kw)
    SHEETS.append(sh)
    return sh


def hole_table(sh, x, y, rows, title='HOLE TABLE', zname='Z'):
    sh.text(x, y - 1.5, title, 3.0, weight='bold')
    cols = [('HOLE', 14, 'middle'), ('X', 18, 'end'), (zname, 18, 'end'), ('DESCRIPTION', 120, 'start')]
    return sh.table(x, y, cols, [[r[0], fmt(r[1]), fmt(r[2]), r[3]] for r in rows], size=2.6, rh=4.4)


def axes_glyph(v, u, w, xlab='X', zlab='Z', down=True):
    x, y = v.P(u, w)
    v.sh.line(x, y, x + 10, y, 'vis'); v.sh.arrow(x + 10, y, 0); v.sh.text(x + 11.5, y + 1, xlab, 2.6)
    v.sh.line(x, y, x, y + (10 if down else -10), 'vis'); v.sh.arrow(x, y + (10 if down else -10), math.pi / 2 if down else -math.pi / 2)
    v.sh.text(x + 1.5, y + (13 if down else -12), zlab, 2.6)
    v.sh.circle(x, y, 1.2, 'vis')


# =====================================================================================
# MP-101 BASE PLATE
# =====================================================================================
def base_outline():
    s = []
    s += [L(-50, -340, 50, -340), A(50, -320, 20, 270, 360), L(70, -320, 70, -140), A(80, -140, 10, 90, 180),
          L(80, -130, 220, -130), A(220, -120, 10, 270, 360), L(230, -120, 230, 120), A(220, 120, 10, 0, 90),
          L(220, 130, -220, 130), A(-220, 120, 10, 90, 180), L(-230, 120, -230, -120), A(-220, -120, 10, 180, 270),
          L(-220, -130, -80, -130), A(-80, -140, 10, 0, 90), L(-70, -140, -70, -320), A(-50, -320, 20, 180, 270)]
    return s


RAIL_F = [-215, -160, -100, -40, 40, 100, 160, 215]
RAIL_B = [-215, -160, -110, -92, -40, 40, 92, 110, 160, 215]


def base_feats():
    f = []
    f.append(feat(0, -105, 'hole', d=20, thru=True, cb=(33, 4.5), cbside='bot', label='C1'))
    f.append(feat(0, 105, 'hole', d=20, thru=True, cb=(33, 4.5), cbside='bot', label='C2'))
    n = 1
    for x in RAIL_F:
        f.append(feat(x, 82, 'tap', m='M5', thru=True, label='R%d' % n)); n += 1
    for x in RAIL_B:
        f.append(feat(x, -82, 'tap', m='M5', thru=True, label='R%d' % n, ldy=-1.6 if x not in (-92, 92) else 4)); n += 1
    n = 1
    for (x, z) in [(-200, -110), (200, -110), (-200, 110), (200, 110), (-55, 320), (55, 320)]:
        f.append(feat(x, z, 'tap', m='M6', thru=True, label='F%d' % n)); n += 1
    f.append(feat(-80, 45, 'spot', d=4, depth=1.5, label='D1'))
    f.append(feat(80, 45, 'spot', d=4, depth=1.5, label='D2'))
    return f


def mp101():
    sh = new('MP-101', 'BASE PLATE', scale='1:2.5', qty='1',
             material='S235JR steel plate 16 mm, profile cut, faced to 12.0',
             finish='Black powder coat 60–80 µm; mask top face inside rails, bores, threads, counterbores',
             notes=['Blank: profile-cut 16 mm S235JR. Face both sides to 12.0 ±0.1. Flatness 0.05 over slide area X ±230 × Z ±75.',
                    'Top face in slide area Ra 1.6 and left unpainted (oil). The die table slides directly on it.',
                    'C1/C2 Ø20 H7 at 210.00 ±0.01 pitch: machine with the same datum and program as crown MP-108 and ram MP-109.',
                    'Hole positions from datum O (midpoint of C1–C2). X to the right; Z toward the front (tongue).',
                    'C1/C2: counterbore Ø33 × 4.5 deep from the BOTTOM for the column clamp washer.',
                    'D1/D2: Ø4 × 90° countersink spot 1.5 deep, top face (ball-plunger detents for die table stations).',
                    ] + GEN)
    v = View(sh, 125, 80, 2.5)
    v.segs(base_outline())
    fs = base_feats()
    draw_plan_features(v, fs)
    v.cl_h(-240, 240, 0); v.cl_v(140, -350, 0)
    axes_glyph(v, 0, 0)
    v.text(0, 0, 'O', 3.0, 'start', dx=-5, dy=-1.8, weight='bold')
    v.hdim(-230, 120, 230, 120, 152)
    v.hdim(-70, -330, 70, -330, -362)
    v.vdim(130, -220, -130, -220, -252)
    v.vdim(130, -220, -340, -60, -270)
    v.vdim(-130, 70, -340, 70, 100)
    v.vdim(105, 0, -105, 0, -150, text='210 ±0.01')
    v.leader(220, 120, 8, -10, '4× R10', on_circle_r=0)
    v.leader(50, -320, 12, 8, '2× R20', on_circle_r=0)
    v.leader(80, -140, 22, 4, '2× R10 fillet', on_circle_r=0)
    v.leader(0, -105, -26, -18, 'C1, C2: Ø20 H7 THRU\nCBORE Ø33 × 4.5 FROM BOTTOM', on_circle_r=10)
    v.text(0, -350, 'PLAN (TOP FACE)', 3.4, dy=14, weight='bold')
    rows = []
    for f in fs:
        if f['kind'] == 'hole':
            d = 'Ø20 H7 THRU; CBORE Ø33 × 4.5 BOTTOM'
        elif f['kind'] == 'tap':
            d = '%s THRU (rail screws)' % f['m'] if f['m'] == 'M5' else '%s THRU (feet)' % f['m']
        else:
            d = 'Ø4 × 90° spot, 1.5 deep (detent)'
        rows.append((f['label'], f['x'], f['z'], d))
    hole_table(sh, 238, 18, rows)
    # detail section through C2
    vd = View(sh, 300, 205, 1.0)
    T = 12
    feats_c2 = [feat(0, 0, 'hole', d=20, thru=True, cb=(33, 4.5), cbside='bot')]
    draw_section(vd, [(-35, 35)], T, feats_c2, 0, y0=0)
    vd.line(-35, 0, -35, T, 'thin'); vd.line(35, 0, 35, T, 'thin')
    vd.cl_v(-4, T + 4, 0)
    vd.hdim(-10, T, 10, T, T + 7, text='Ø20 H7')
    vd.hdim(-16.5, 0, 16.5, 0, -6, text='Ø33')
    vd.vdim(0, 35, T, 35, 43, text='12')
    vd.vdim(0, -16.5, 4.5, -16.5, -24, text='4.5')
    vd.text(0, 0, 'DETAIL SECTION THROUGH C1/C2  (1:1)', 3.0, dy=10, weight='bold')
    dx = DXF(); dx.segs(base_outline()); feats_dxf(dx, fs); DXFS['MP-101_base_plate.dxf'] = dx


# =====================================================================================
# MP-102 GUIDE RAIL, MP-103 KEEPER
# =====================================================================================
def mp102():
    sh = new('MP-102', 'GUIDE RAIL', scale='1:2', qty='2 (1 × -F, 1 × -B)',
             material='C45 bright flat 16 × 14, ground to 14 × 12.05',
             finish='Black oxide; ground faces oiled',
             notes=['Height 12.05 ±0.01: equal to die table MP-105 thickness + 0.05 running clearance. Grind both rails together.',
                    'Ground faces: top, bottom and inner face (faces the die table). Inner face straight within 0.02 over 460.',
                    'Variant -F: front rail, 8 holes. Variant -B: back rail, 10 holes (includes stop-block screws).',
                    'Holes Ø5.5 THRU on the rail centreline; hole X positions measured from the rail centre.'] + GEN)
    for i, (var, xs, oy) in enumerate([('-F (front)', RAIL_F, 60), ('-B (back)', RAIL_B, 150)]):
        v = View(sh, 150, oy, 2.0)
        v.rect(-230, -7, 230, 7)
        for x in xs:
            v.circle(x, 0, 2.75); v.cmark(x, 0, 2.75)
        v.cl_h(-236, 236, 0)
        v.text(-230, 7, 'MP-102%s  TOP VIEW' % var.split()[0], 3.2, 'start', dy=-9, weight='bold')
        v.hdim(-230, -7, 230, -7, -24)
        v.vdim(7, 230, -7, 230, 238, text='14')
        # front view under top view
        vf = View(sh, 150, oy + 30, 2.0)
        vf.rect(-230, 0, 230, 12.05)
        for x in xs:
            vf.line(x - 2.75, 0, x - 2.75, 12.05, 'hid'); vf.line(x + 2.75, 0, x + 2.75, 12.05, 'hid')
        vf.vdim(0, 230, 12.05, 230, 238, text='12.05 ±0.01')
        sh.text(300, oy - 6, 'Hole X positions (from rail centre), all Ø5.5 THRU:', 2.8, weight='bold')
        sh.text(300, oy, ', '.join(fmt(x) for x in xs), 2.8)
    dx = DXF(); dx.segs(rrect(0, 0, 460, 14, 0)); [dx.segs([C(x, 0, 2.75)], 'HOLES') for x in RAIL_F]; DXFS['MP-102-F_guide_rail_front.dxf'] = dx
    dx = DXF(); dx.segs(rrect(0, 0, 460, 14, 0)); [dx.segs([C(x, 0, 2.75)], 'HOLES') for x in RAIL_B]; DXFS['MP-102-B_guide_rail_back.dxf'] = dx


def mp103():
    sh = new('MP-103', 'KEEPER STRIP (GIB)', scale='1:2', qty='2 (1 × -F, 1 × -B)',
             material='C45 bright flat 20 × 4',
             finish='Black oxide',
             notes=['Sits on top of the guide rail and overlaps the die table edge by 5 mm (inner edge).',
                    'Countersunk holes: Ø5.5 THRU, 90° countersink to Ø10.4 (for M5 ISO 10642), from top.',
                    'Variant -B: four plain Ø5.5 holes at X ±92 and ±110 for the stop-block screws (no countersink).',
                    'Hole line 12.0 from the inner edge. Hole X positions measured from the strip centre.'] + GEN)
    for (var, csk, plain, oy) in [('-F (front)', RAIL_F, [], 60), ('-B (back)', [-215, -160, -40, 40, 160, 215], [-110, -92, 92, 110], 150)]:
        v = View(sh, 150, oy, 2.0)
        v.rect(-230, -10, 230, 10)
        for x in csk:
            v.circle(x, -2, 2.75); v.circle(x, -2, 5.2); v.cmark(x, -2, 5.2)
        for x in plain:
            v.circle(x, -2, 2.75); v.cmark(x, -2, 2.75)
        v.text(-230, 10, 'MP-103%s  TOP VIEW  (inner edge at bottom)' % var.split()[0], 3.2, 'start', dy=-9, weight='bold')
        v.hdim(-230, -10, 230, -10, -26)
        v.vdim(10, 230, -10, 230, 238, text='20')
        v.vdim(-2, -230, -10, -230, -240, text='12')
        vf = View(sh, 150, oy + 32, 2.0)
        vf.rect(-230, 0, 230, 4)
        vf.vdim(0, 230, 4, 230, 238, text='4')
        sh.text(300, oy - 6, 'Countersunk (M5 ISO 10642):', 2.8, weight='bold')
        sh.text(300, oy, ', '.join(fmt(x) for x in csk), 2.8)
        if plain:
            sh.text(300, oy + 6, 'Plain Ø5.5 THRU:', 2.8, weight='bold')
            sh.text(300, oy + 12, ', '.join(fmt(x) for x in plain), 2.8)


# =====================================================================================
# MP-104 STOP BLOCK, MP-106 STOP PIN
# =====================================================================================
def mp104():
    sh = new('MP-104', 'STATION STOP BLOCK', scale='2:1', qty='2',
             material='C45 bright 30 × 16 flat',
             finish='Black oxide',
             notes=['Bolted through keeper MP-103-B and rail MP-102-B into the base with 2 × M5 × 35 ISO 4762.',
                    'Stop screw: M6 × 0.75 × 25 hex screw + thin lock nut (bought). Nominal protrusion 3 mm from the inner face.',
                    'The 7 mm overhang (Z 20–27) sits above the die table; the table stop pin MP-106 hits the screw tip.',
                    'Z measured from the back face (the face over the keeper).'] + GEN)
    # top view: u = x (30), w = -z' ; z' from back face 0..27 -> w from 0 (back, top) to -27
    v = View(sh, 90, 50, 0.5)
    v.rect(-15, 0, 15, -27)
    for x in (-9, 9):
        v.circle(x, -8, 2.75); v.circle(x, -8, 4.75); v.cmark(x, -8, 4.75)
    v.line(-15, -22 - 2.6, 15, -22 - 2.6, 'hid'); v.line(-15, -22 + 2.6, 15, -22 + 2.6, 'hid'); v.cl_h(-18, 18, -22)
    v.text(0, 0, 'TOP VIEW', 3.2, dy=-14, weight='bold')
    v.hdim(-15, 0, 15, 0, 9)
    v.hdim(-9, -8, 9, -8, -40, text='18')
    v.vdim(0, -15, -27, -15, -24, text='27')
    v.vdim(0, 15, -8, 15, 22, text='8')
    v.vdim(0, 15, -22, 15, 30, text='22')
    v.leader(9, -8, 18, -16, '2× Ø5.5 THRU\nCBORE Ø9.5 × 5.5', on_circle_r=4.75)
    # front view (x, y)
    vf = View(sh, 90, 150, 0.5)
    vf.rect(-15, 0, 15, 16)
    for x in (-9, 9):
        vf.line(x - 2.75, 0, x - 2.75, 10.5, 'hid'); vf.line(x + 2.75, 0, x + 2.75, 10.5, 'hid')
        vf.line(x - 4.75, 10.5, x - 4.75, 16, 'hid'); vf.line(x + 4.75, 10.5, x + 4.75, 16, 'hid'); vf.line(x - 4.75, 10.5, x + 4.75, 10.5, 'hid')
    vf.line(-15, 8 - 2.6, 15, 8 - 2.6, 'hid'); vf.line(-15, 8 + 2.6, 15, 8 + 2.6, 'hid'); vf.cl_h(-18, 18, 8)
    vf.text(0, 0, 'FRONT VIEW (from the die table side)', 3.2, dy=14, weight='bold')
    vf.vdim(0, -15, 16, -15, -24, text='16')
    vf.vdim(0, 15, 8, 15, 22, text='8')
    # side view (z', y) showing tapped hole end-on
    vs = View(sh, 230, 150, 0.5)
    vs.rect(0, 0, 27, 16)
    vs.circle(22, 8, MINOR['M6x0.75'] / 2); vs.thread_arc(22, 8, 3.0); vs.cmark(22, 8, 3)
    vs.text(13.5, 0, 'SIDE VIEW', 3.2, dy=14, weight='bold')
    vs.hdim(0, 16, 27, 16, 25)
    vs.leader(22, 8, 20, -22, 'M6 × 0.75 THRU (along X)', on_circle_r=3)
    vs.hdim(0, 0, 22, 0, -9, text='22')


def mp106():
    sh = new('MP-106', 'DIE TABLE STOP PIN', scale='4:1', qty='1',
             material='C45 Ø8 bright bar',
             finish='Harden 45–50 HRC; black oxide',
             notes=['Screwed into the die table (MP-105, hole S) with Loctite 243.', 'Contact face Ø6 must be square to the axis within 0.05.'] + GEN)
    v = View(sh, 120, 110, 0.25)
    v.rect(0, -3, 16, 3); v.rect(-6, -2, 0, 2)
    v.line(-6, -1.65, 0, -1.65, 'thin'); v.line(-6, 1.65, 0, 1.65, 'thin')
    v.cl_h(-9, 19, 0)
    v.hdim(0, 3, 16, 3, 8)
    v.hdim(-6, 2, 0, 2, 8, text='6')
    v.vdim(-3, 8, 3, 8, 21, text='Ø6')
    v.leader(-3, -2, -8, 12, 'M4 × 6')
    v.text(5, -3, 'SIDE VIEW', 3.2, dy=24, weight='bold')


# =====================================================================================
# MP-105 DIE TABLE
# =====================================================================================
def table_feats():
    f = [feat(-125, -57, 'hole', d=8, depth=10, label='DA1'), feat(-35, -57, 'hole', d=8, depth=10, label='DA2'),
         feat(50, 57, 'hole', d=8, depth=10, label='DB1'), feat(110, 57, 'hole', d=8, depth=10, label='DB2'),
         feat(-17, 55, 'tap', m='M5', thru=True, label='T1'), feat(-143, -55, 'tap', m='M5', thru=True, label='T2'),
         feat(143, 55, 'tap', m='M5', thru=True, label='T3'), feat(17, -55, 'tap', m='M5', thru=True, label='T4'),
         feat(0, -66, 'tap', m='M4', depth=8, label='S'), feat(0, 45, 'tap', m='M6', thru=True, label='P')]
    return f


def mp105():
    sh = new('MP-105', 'DIE TABLE (SLIDE)', scale='1:2', qty='1',
             material='EN AW-6061-T6 plate 15 mm, faced to 12.00',
             finish='Hard anodise 25 µm, gold; fit Helicoils after anodising',
             notes=['Thickness 12.00 ±0.01 and flat within 0.03 after anodising. Guide rails MP-102 are 12.05.',
                    'Station A dowels DA1/DA2 lie on a line parallel to X; station B dowels DB1/DB2 use a different pitch so the A and B die shoes cannot be swapped.',
                    'DA/DB: Ø8 H7 × 10 deep (after anodise). T1–T4: tap STI M5 for M5 × 1D Helicoil, THRU. S: M4 × 8 for stop pin MP-106.',
                    'P: M6 THRU for M6 spring ball plunger (detents D1/D2 in the base). K1/K2: M6 × 12 in each end face, centred, for push knobs.',
                    'Hole positions from the table centre. Station centres at X = −80 (A) and +80 (B), Z = 0.',
                    'Long edges: 0.5 × 45° chamfer only (they run against the rails).'] + GEN)
    v = View(sh, 115, 65, 2.0)
    v.segs(rrect(0, 0, 340, 150, 0))
    fs = table_feats()
    draw_plan_features(v, fs)
    v.cl_h(-175, 175, 0); v.cl_v(80, -80, 0)
    for x in (-80, 80):
        v.cl_v(70, -70, x); v.text(x, 0, 'STATION ' + ('A' if x < 0 else 'B'), 2.6, dy=-2)
    axes_glyph(v, 0, 0)
    v.hdim(-170, 75, 170, 75, 95)
    v.vdim(75, -170, -75, -170, -190)
    v.hdim(-80, 75, 80, 75, 85, text='160')
    v.text(0, -75, 'PLAN', 3.4, dy=12, weight='bold')
    rows = []
    for f in fs:

# Turned-part helper
# =====================================================================================
def turned(sh, ox, oy, scale, segs):
    v = View(sh, ox, oy, scale)
    x = 0.0
    pos = []
    for s in segs:
        r = s['d'] / 2.0
        if s.get('groove'):
            r = s['d'] / 2.0
        v.line(x, r, x + s['l'], r); v.line(x, -r, x + s['l'], -r)
        if s.get('thread'):
            mr = MINOR[s['thread']] / 2.0
            v.line(x, mr, x + s['l'], mr, 'thin'); v.line(x, -mr, x + s['l'], -mr, 'thin')
        pos.append((x, x + s['l'], r))
        x += s['l']
    for i, (a, b, r) in enumerate(pos):
        rp = pos[i - 1][2] if i > 0 else 0
        v.line(a, -max(r, rp), a, max(r, rp))
    v.line(x, -pos[-1][2], x, pos[-1][2])
    v.cl_h(-5, x + 5, 0)
    return v, pos, x


def tapped_end(v, xend, m, thread_depth, inward=1):
    """draw a tapped hole into an end face at u=xend going in direction inward (+1 right, -1 left)."""
    mn, mj = MINOR[m] / 2, MAJOR[m] / 2
    drill = thread_depth + MAJOR[m] * 0.4
    e1 = xend + inward * thread_depth; e2 = xend + inward * drill
    v.line(xend, mn, e2, mn, 'hid'); v.line(xend, -mn, e2, -mn, 'hid')
    v.line(xend, mj, e1, mj, 'hid'); v.line(xend, -mj, e1, -mj, 'hid')
    v.line(e1, -mj, e1, mj, 'hid')
    tip = e2 + inward * mn * 0.6
    v.line(e2, mn, tip, 0, 'hid'); v.line(e2, -mn, tip, 0, 'hid')
